item.title: Tourism, remittances support spending as investment surges: RBF
item.description: Strong tourism activity and remittance inflows are continuing to support consumer spending in Fiji, while investment indicators are pointing to increased economic activity, according to the Reserve Bank of Fiji’s August Economic Review. Consumption-related lending grew by 1.2 per cent in the year to July, driven mainly by a 14.3 per cent increase in lending to private individuals.
item.content:encoded:
Strong tourism activity and remittance inflows are continuing to support consumer spending in Fiji, while investment indicators are pointing to increased economic activity, according to the Reserve Bank of Fiji’s August Economic Review.

Consumption-related lending grew by 1.2 per cent in the year to July, driven mainly by a 14.3 per cent increase in lending to private individuals.

Vehicle registrations also increased by 9.9 per cent, with new vehicle registrations rising 12.9 per cent and second-hand registrations up 7.5 per cent.

However, the RBF warned that higher import duties on new and second-hand vehicles announced in the 2026-27 National Budget could weigh on vehicle demand going forward.

Investment activity also remained positive. New investment lending surged by 38.3 per cent in the year to July, driven largely by increased lending to the building and construction sector, which rose 67.7 per cent, and real estate, which increased 34.7 per cent.

Domestic cement sales recorded strong growth of 38.2 per cent, reflecting sustained demand from ongoing development projects.

Construction-related imports also increased by 20.6 per cent up to May, supported by increased construction activity and growing use of prefabricated building materials.

The RBF said financial conditions remained supportive of economic activity, with ample liquidity in the banking system and low interest rates.

Banking system liquidity stood at approximately $2.1 billion as of August 28, helping keep borrowing costs low.

Both commercial banks’ weighted average new and outstanding lending rates stood at 4.50 per cent in July.

The accommodative financial conditions also supported strong private sector credit growth of 14.6 per cent.

Broad money expanded by 7.8 per cent in July, reflecting continued growth in liquidity and credit within the economy.

The latest indicators suggest domestic demand remains resilient, with tourism and remittances supporting household spending while construction, real estate and other investment activity continue to expand.

item.title: The Fiji Times marks 157 years of documenting Fiji’s journey
item.description: The Fiji Times is marking its 157th birthday, with Editor-in-Chief Fred Wesley reflecting on the newspaper’s beginnings and its enduring role in documenting Fiji’s history. Wesley said three significant events in the newspaper’s history helped give birth to an idea that would eventually become one of Fiji’s longest-running institutions.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Times is marking its 157th birthday, with Editor-in-Chief Fred Wesley reflecting on the newspaper’s beginnings and its enduring role in documenting Fiji’s history.

Wesley said three significant events in the newspaper’s history helped give birth to an idea that would eventually become one of Fiji’s longest-running institutions.

He began with the life of founder George Littleton Griffiths, who was born in London on July 29, 1844, as the eldest of six children.

Griffiths later travelled to New Zealand and worked as a compositor for Mills, Dick & Co. in Port Chalmers, Dunedin.

But Wesley said Griffiths could have remained in New Zealand and chosen a different path.

Instead, in early 1869, he left Port Lyttelton in Christchurch and travelled to Levuka, where the journey of The Fiji Times began.

“London and New Zealand were worlds away from the little sleepy town of Levuka,” Wesley said.

“He could have opted to stay there. But no!” Wesley said Griffiths arrived in Levuka at a time when settlers were taking early steps towards nationhood and establishing some form of governance.

He recalled comments made by former Fiji Times editor, the late Sir Len Usher, on October 15, 1962, drawing from the Cyclopaedia of Fiji.

“In 1869, when Mr Griffith landed in Levuka, there was no form of government whatsoever,” Wesley quoted.

Usher noted that despite the lack of formal government and the freedom enjoyed by settlers, the community was relatively orderly, with the press playing an important role in maintaining order.

“For the first two years… the press played an important part in the preservation of order,” Wesley said.

Wesley said The Fiji Times had since become closely intertwined with the story of Fiji itself.

“Today, we celebrate our 157th birthday. It is an opportunity to reflect on our history which documents the story of Fiji,” he said.

“Through the pages of The Fiji Times, we have seen the birth of a nation and how it has developed over the years.”

He said the newspaper had chronicled Fiji’s transition and transformation, reporting on moments of national achievement as well as periods of difficulty and uncertainty.

“We have seen the good, the bad and the ugly. We have shared in the joys of national achievements and felt sadness together,” Wesley said.

He also paid tribute to the resilience of Fijians, particularly during times of national disasters.

“Through all of this, we have also seen and were amazed about the resilience of Fijians in times of national disasters,” he said.

Wesley said The Fiji Times had also remained committed to the fundamental principles of journalism, including holding those in power to account.

“Today, we maintain our commitment to being part of the development of our nation. Together,” he said.

item.title: Vosarogo hits back at Narube over CRC criticism
item.description: Minister for Lands and Mineral Resources Filimoni Vosarogo has accused Unity Fiji leader Savenaca Narube of spreading a false and irresponsible narrative about Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s response to the Constitutional Review Commission report. Vosarogo said he was concerned by Narube’s suggestion that the Prime Minister had deliberately used the CRC report to create fear and uncertainty arou
item.content:encoded:
Minister for Lands and Mineral Resources Filimoni Vosarogo has accused Unity Fiji leader Savenaca Narube of spreading a false and irresponsible narrative about Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s response to the Constitutional Review Commission report.

Vosarogo said he was concerned by Narube’s suggestion that the Prime Minister had deliberately used the CRC report to create fear and uncertainty around race and religion for political gain.

He said the allegation was not supported by evidence and misrepresented the Prime Minister’s message to the nation.

“Contrary to Narube’s false narrative, the Prime Minister did not spread hate. He did not spread fear. He did not threaten any community,” Vosarogo said.

Vosarogo said Rabuka’s opening appeal for Fijians to remain calm was made in response to racial and religious rhetoric already circulating online. He said Narube’s comments were particularly irresponsible given the sensitivity of race and religion in Fiji.

“The irony should not be lost on anyone. The Prime Minister specifically appealed to political leaders to be responsible with their words and not turn this national discussion into a political, racial or religious battle,” he said.

Vosarogo said Narube’s response had instead risked doing exactly what the Prime Minister had warned against.

Narube had said there was “no need to fracture this beautiful country again”, a comment Vosarogo said was advice the Unity Fiji leader should also follow.

“Through this kind of false and irresponsible nonsense, he himself appears to be attempting to fracture our nation,” Vosarogo said.

He urged Fijians to read Rabuka’s statement for themselves and form their own conclusions about what the Prime Minister had said.

Vosarogo said political leaders could disagree, criticise and debate different visions for Fiji, but there should be a limit when race and religion were brought into political attacks based on claims he described as untrue.

“Fiji deserves a political discourse that is robust, but responsible,” he said.

“Those who seek to lead this country have a duty to contribute to that standard, not undermine it.” Vosarogo’s statement comes amid heightened public discussion following the release of the CRC’s review of the 2013 Constitution and its proposed Draft Constitution of the Republic of Fiji 2026.

item.title: RBF: Job advertisements fall 30.5% as formal employment grows
item.description: Fiji’s labour market is showing mixed signals, with job advertisements falling sharply while formal employment and wages continue to increase, according to the Reserve Bank of Fiji’s August Economic Review. Newspaper job advertisements declined by 30.5 per cent in the first seven months of 2026, reflecting weaker recruitment intentions across most sectors.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s labour market is showing mixed signals, with job advertisements falling sharply while formal employment and wages continue to increase, according to the Reserve Bank of Fiji’s August Economic Review.

Newspaper job advertisements declined by 30.5 per cent in the first seven months of 2026, reflecting weaker recruitment intentions across most sectors.

The Reserve Bank said the decline was particularly evident following the Government’s public service hiring freeze, as well as reduced vacancies in the transport, storage and communication, wholesale and retail trade, and business services sectors.

Despite the weaker demand for new workers, formal employment continued to expand.

Formal employment increased by 1.7 per cent to 205,596 workers by June, while total wages paid rose by 7.9 per cent.

The RBF said labour supply was also being affected by increased outward migration.

A total of 1,834 workers left Fiji under outward labour mobility arrangements in the first seven months of the year, an increase of 20 per cent.

The increase was mainly driven by participation in the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme.

Long-term resident departures also increased by 5.9 per cent, with departures for employment rising by 17.2 per cent and those for other purposes increasing by 21.1 per cent.

The figures point to a labour market where fewer new vacancies are being advertised domestically, while existing formal employment remains relatively resilient and more workers are seeking employment opportunities overseas.

item.title: Used syringes among waste removed from Vatuwaqa Creek
item.description: The waste included plastic bottles, food wrappers, household rubbish and plastic bags, with the discovery of used syringes raising particular health and safety concerns for clean-up workers. Minister for Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya said the volume and nature of the waste highlighted the need for people to dispose of rubbish responsibly.
item.content:encoded:
The waste included plastic bottles, food wrappers, household rubbish and plastic bags, with the discovery of used syringes raising particular health and safety concerns for clean-up workers.

Minister for Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya said the volume and nature of the waste highlighted the need for people to dispose of rubbish responsibly.

“What you throw into the drain or creek upstream becomes somebody else’s problem downstream. Eventually, it reaches our rivers and our ocean,” Tabuya said.

She said the used syringes were particularly concerning because of the risks they posed to people involved in removing the waste.

Tabuya also reminded the public that the fixed penalty for littering increased to $200 from September 1 .

“Government can clean this creek today, but if people dump rubbish again tomorrow, we are back to square one,” she said.

The Ministry acknowledged Trashboom Pacific and community members who assisted with the clean-up.

Tabuya urged the public to help keep drains, creeks, rivers and the ocean free of waste.
